Morgan Stanley
Summer Analyst Interview Experience
Rupak R. Gupta (RRG)
B. Tech. Information Technology
Batch 2027
Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute (VJTI)

The Morgan Stanley Experience
Overview
During our 2025 TY internship drive, the company that arrived near the beginning of August was Morgan
Stanley. The online assessment (OA) was scheduled for the 10th of August, while the pre-placement talk
(PPT) was scheduled on the 11th of August. The process from the arrival of the company to the final
shortlists took almost an entire week.
Eligibility Criteria
The eligibility criteria for Morgan Stanley is,
1. Circuital Branch (Computer Engineering, Information Technology, E-branches)
2. CGPA ≥7.5
3. No active backlogs
Online Assessment
Date: 10th August, 2025
Platform: SHL AMCAT (No Proctoring)
Duration: 2 hours
The online assessment was held on the SHL AMCAT platform. It had an overall duration of 120 minutes
(lasting from 14:00 to 16:00) and consisted of three sections: Debugging, Aptitude and Programming.
Each section was separately timed; you had to complete one section for the entire stipulated duration before
moving onto the next. This also meant that once the duration of a section was over, it was not possible to
return to a previous section.
Below are the descriptions of the individual sections.
Page 1 of 12

Section 1: Debugging
Duration: ∼20 minutes
Allowed Programming Languages: Only C++ or Java
This sections consisted of a lightning round of simple programming problems where an implementation of the
code was already given, albeit intentionally buggy. The objective of the round was to “assess the candidate’s
ability to diagnose and identify any bugs in the code and fix them”.
The round consisted of around 7 or so problems, all very introductory programming programs such as sorting,
searching or if-else problems. An example I recall from memory is:
1
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
2
for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++);
3
System.out.print("*");
4
System.out.println();
5
}
In the above problem, not only is there an off-by-one error (j <= i), but also the inner loop body ends early
because of the stray semicolon (for (int j = 0; j <= i; j++);).
Another example was a case where an implementation of selection sort was provided, but it was returning
the contents in the reverse order than what was expected. A bit of digging around with the comparisons
allowed fixing of this one.
What is worth noting is that the only languages allowed in this section are C++ or Java. I reckon this is
because of their universal curly brace and semicolon syntax. I personally had better experience with Java, so
I solved all problems in that.
Section 2: Aptitude
Duration: ∼40 minutes
This was probably the meat and potatoes of the entire assessment. This section had a mixed set of interactive
and MCQ-style problems. The theme of the questions was logical reasoning and data interpretation.
While the exact questions themselves are lost to time, here is a gist of the kind of problems asked:
• Logical scheduling: Meeting schedules given for a bunch of employees, and a map of an office
consisting of multiple departments. Each employee and department have their own availability windows
and conflicts, and our objective was to align the employees to have a non-conflicting schedule. The
interaction to this problem was also fun, as we had to literally drag-and-drop the employee to the
correct department using the mouse on the map.
• Logical ordering: Some riddle-like clues such as “A is faster than B with one in between” and “C is
slower than D” are provided; we have to drag-and-drop the entities to rank them in the correct order.
• Pattern recognition: A very typical olympiad-style problem where three esoteric images are provided,
and you gotta pick the next likely image in the sequence.
• Data interpretation: A description of some companies’ finances is provided, and we had to interactively
resize a pie chart or reorder a bar chart to match the exact percentages of the finances in the correct
categories.
This section had the most problems, which was around 15 to 20 of them. I personally could not finish some
Page 2 of 12

of the last few problems in time, but as we shall see later, it still worked out.
Section 3: Programming
Duration: ∼60 minutes
Allowed Programming Languages: Any
This section is the typical programming round, where three DSA problems were asked, not dissimilar to a
CodeChef or Codeforces contest.
Unlike the debugging round, all well-known programming languages were allowed here predictably, and I
chose to go with Python; being the language I had the most experience with in Competitive Programming.
Here are the descriptions of the three problems, best recalled from memory:
1. Given an array of order sizes, which is intended to be sorted in ascending order, find the number of orders
which are currently in their incorrect positions. The approach was very simple, as it only required a
comparison of the given array with its sorted version.
2. An array of 𝑁numeric IDs are given of the same digit length. The problem essentially asked to count
the sum of the number of distinct digits in the same position across all pairs of the IDs array. While
this seems daunting, and some optimized approaches may come to mind, a brute-force solution was
actually accepted by the judge.
3. There are 𝑀sprints and 𝑁events. Each sprint is essentially an interval with a start and end time, and
each event should occur at a certain time. The question asked for the number of events that were not
covered by any sprint. Sorting the sprints chronologically and performing a prefix calculation allowed
counting all events that do not get covered by any sprint.
As it can be observed, the judge focused on correctness over optimization. Most brute-force solutions
were acceptable, and thus did not ask too much of the candidates. I was able to get all three problems
cleared with a good 15 minutes still remaining, so I was able to complete the assessment early.
The OA happened on Sunday, and with no results out I was just shopping groceries on Monday evening, only
to be surprised by a congratulatory notification, finding out I was actually shortlisted for the interview that
would occur... the next day. Well that was unexpected.
Not only me, but a grand total of 17 shortlists and 3 waitlists were selected; me being a part of the 17
shortlists.
Page 3 of 12

Interview
The interviews were conducted on the 12th of August, on Zoom. Since the interviews were online, we did not
need the commute to college. The interviews conducted of two rounds: Technical and Human Resources
(HR).
Interview 1: Technical Round
The interviews started at 09:00 in the morning and lasted till 16:30, each interview lasting one hour long.
My position in the queue was #13, and my interview slot itself was at 13:00. This meant that I had to
essentially wait in anticipation from the start of the first interview, frequently revising all topics I could recall.
Now while this section is about the interview itself, I would like to mention my last-day preparation method,
which is outlined in the last section of this document.
Coming to the interview itself, I joined a Zoom waiting call and the first step to begin the interview for a
candidate was to just present a valid government ID via the camera to prove their identity. After that, the
candidate is redirected to the call with their interviewer.
As the interview began, I gave a short introduction of myself, simply stating my current academic and
programming background.
The interviewer requested me to open an IDE or code editor without autocomplete to begin the DSA round.
However, I myself elected to perform the technical round in Google Docs or Word instead, which was also
fine with the interviewer.
My rationale was to mitigate any contemporary issues in the dev environment on my machine, which
could mess up code execution. Other than that I could also showcase programming without intellisense or
autocomplete, which was possible only due to my proficiency in Java, and also dodge the event of subtle
bugs or errors if the code were to be executed. Although I would like to confirm that this is not a required
step (or even a possible step given the interviewer), and if you are comfortable with an IDE, then do so.
First Problem: Left Side View of a Binary Tree
The interviewer properly began the technical round by asking me whether I “had the knowledge of tree data
structures”. I affirmed and she was able to provide the first DSA problem: Left Side View of a Binary Tree.
The problem presented a rooted binary tree which if were to be looked from the left side, would produce a
list of vertices that are visible. This is a variation on the LeetCode problem 199 External-Link-Alt.
I solved all DSA problems in Java, as it was the language I had the most confidence with. I explained the
method leftSideView(...) that would input the root of the tree as an argument, and verbally constructed
my logic as I coded along the solution.
I opted for a recursive solution (DFS), as is the case for binary tree-based problems. An interesting quirk of
that approach was me wanting an initial condition on the first call, because of which I opted to overload the
above method with an additional height parameter. This very decision prompted the interviewer to ask
what I understood by “overloading”, starting a tangent of OOP/Java questions in the midst of the DSA
problem. The questions best recalled from memory were:
• What is method overloading?
• What is the difference between ‘overloading’ and ‘overriding’?
Page 4 of 12

Third Problem: Querying non-retired employees
The next topic was of databases and SQL. The setup was two tables: employees and retired_employees
in a relational database with the same schema:
1
first_name TEXT
2
last_name TEXT
3
age INTEGER
4
salary REAL
5
dept TEXT
The problem was to obtain the full names of the non-retired employees with salary greater than 50,000,
age less than 20, and dept of ‘XYZ’.
Simply obtaining the first and last names given the condition in either table is trivial. The curveball was to
exclude all the employees that existed in the retired table from the employees queried from the first table.
I personally first constructed the trivial query to fetch the employee names with the given specifications, and
then used the set MINUS operator. The other nitpick was to have a single column full_name derived from
first_name and last_name. I pretty much threw the CONCAT operator at the end of my query, and the
interviewer accepted the result.
This was the query I had presented:
1
(
2
SELECT CONCAT(first_name , last_name) AS full_name
3
FROM employees
4
WHERE salary > 50000
5
AND age < 20
6
AND dept = 'XYZ'
7
) MINUS (
8
SELECT CONCAT(first_name , last_name) AS full_name
9
FROM retired_employees
10
WHERE salary > 50000
11
AND age < 20
12
AND dept = 'XYZ'
13
);
Note that the CONCAT operator may be used incorrectly here. This should reinforce that the objective of
an interview is not to always be 100% correct1 in terms of code; it is to be able to present your logic and
thinking clearly.
Apart from the SQL problem the interviewer also transitioned into some DBMS questions, which were as
follows:
• What are joins?
• What is the difference between a LEFT JOIN and a LEFT OUTER JOIN?
Note: I was unable to answer this question, as this was a trick question: there is no semantic difference
between the two.
1While this theme was very ingrained in this interview, the tolerance of “correctness” may change with the company or even
the interviewer.
Page 7 of 12

Interview 2: HR Round
My initial interview had ended by 14:00, and by the next hour the shortlists for the next round had arrived:
3 shortlists from the original 17 and the 3 waitlists were also revealed for their first round, who were unknown
so far. As the technical rounds continued in parallel, few more people were eligible for the HR round.
My HR interview was due in the next 30 minutes from the time of the update. I did not have much to
prepare as such, and opted to surf through commonly asked questions.
The interview began with my introduction, and I pretty much explained my academic and programming
background the same way as the first time, but the outcome was different. First of all, the interviewer was
simply curious about VJTI and the relation of its autonomy with Mumbai University. I explained the history
of the institute off the top of my head.
Another attribute I had mentioned in my intro was my CGPA, which was over 9 at the time. This prompted
a question by the interviewer:
“If people like Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman are dropouts, then why would you feel the need to
mention your CGPA?”
This was a tough question, as one of the pillars to hold in an on-campus internship is a high GPA. I tackled
it by justifying that while people may succeed regardless of GPA, being able to actually maintain a high GPA
over all the semesters does prove a candidate’s consistency and effort. I also pointed out Morgan Stanley’s
own 7.5+ CGPA criteria, which existed to prove a candidate had put in the effort to maintain that score.
Another description I mentioned about me was my participation in student clubs, primarily Project X and the
CP Club. The interviewer was intrigued by the CP Club and asked what it is and what role I played in it.
This provided me an opportunity to praise the mentoring culture of VJTI and its application in the CP Club.
Continuing on with the CP Club, I also described the ICPC as it was related. Not only that, I also mentioned
about me participating in the ICPC of 2025, which helped me make a stronger impression on the interviewer.
This was technically true, as I did appear for the ICPC prelims later that year.
After the introduction was over, the interviewer asked me about AI-assisted coding, and if I used any tools
for those myself at the time. I mentioned the name of an LLM-based IDE I had used, and the interviewer
was impressed, as the company behind that software had good relations with Morgan Stanley. This was
completely unintentional though, but it sure was a pleasant surprise.
Continuing on with the topic, the interviewer presented the first proper question:
“Where would you see yourself in five years if LLMs generate all code?”
Since I had used LLMs for coding myself, I was somewhat prepared for the question. My answer in a gist
was explaining the fact that engineers are problem solvers; not code writers. Not only that, the imaginative
skills of humans can fundamentally not be replaced with AI, or at least not in those next five years.
Ultimately I presented my own independent views on the topic, which is what is expected of a candidate in
an HR interview. Thus, there is no need to consider any of these answers as templates; treat them more as
guidelines to think of your answer. Always remember the only person the interviewer wants to see is ‘you’.
Having said that, I will now list down the remaining questions that were asked to me upon which I presented
my own thoughts.
• What are you planning to do after your four years of engineering?
Page 8 of 12

• What are three of your non-negotiables?
Note: These are your own non-negotiables, that you adopt in your life.
• How would you handle a conflict within a team?
Circling back to the discussion on GPAs, here was another fun question asked:
• If someone with a lower grade is in conflict with you, how would you win the argument?
This is another kind of a trick question, as there is no real correlation between a person’s academic grade
and the matter of a conflict.
After all these questions, the HR round was pretty much over. The interviewer asked me for any questions
I had for the firm, and I connected a research experience I had in my profile to the question and inquired
of Research and Development (RnD) in the firm. The interviewer explained a lot about the firm and what
many of its sectors do. It was a pleasant conversation.
And that word is important: Conversation. Never did I feel I was necessarily getting ‘tested’, as I was simply
responding instinctively with the answers and opinions I already had. I felt genuinely confident that I had
performed well.
Results
Unlike other company experiences, there was actually some waiting for the Morgan Stanley results. This was
because 2 of the waitlisted candidates were actually eligible for the second interview round, but the time of
the day had run out. This induced a second set of interviews only for the two remaining candidates the next
day (Wednesday), and the day after that (Thursday) was when the results got announced within college
hours itself: 4 people were accepted, of which I was one!
Resources
Here are a few resources I personally used during my preparation, although the list is very flexible:
Youtube Java Full Course by Bro Code
External-Link-Alt LeetCode Top 150
External-Link-Alt Interviewbit — Technical Interview Questions
External-Link-Alt CodeHelp Core CS Notes
External-Link-Alt CodeChef Starters
External-Link-Alt Codeforces Rounds
♥My peers
Do practice coding problems under time constraints; contests like those of CodeChef and Codeforces provide
very similar environments to OAs which can help preparation.
Researching and preparing using LLMs is also recommended, as for the most part one can get accurate
information about core CS and also tailor the chat according to their preferences.
Page 9 of 12

Behind the Scenes
This was surely a whole lot of a process for one internship. But the reality is that none of this existed
in a vacuum: Everyone who had to wait till Morgan Stanley on-campus had essentially “failed” six or so
companies already, including JPMorgan Chase & Co., D. E. Shaw & Co., Goldman Sachs, Bank of New York
Mellon and others.
It is easy to read this experience and assume things went hunky-dory, while in reality it was a very stressful
and meticulous process. While I personally do not like labeling companies as ‘good’ or ‘bad’, one metric
a lot of people use is the pay. Higher-paying companies, on average, are expected to arrive early, while
lower-paying companies tend to arrive on-campus later, although there is no guarantee to this rule.
Keeping this in mind, imagine a student not making into any company early on and they observe their
opportunities gradually thinning out. I was a victim of this very scenario.
I personally could not clear the OAs for any of the first few companies. The first company I did succeed in
was Pattern, an e-commerce accelerator. I was a waitlist interviewee, which induced my slot of the first round
to the very end, making me wait till late evening inside the campus. It was all for naught, as I butchered the
interview.
The next company in-line before Morgan Stanley was BNY Mellon. I had an okayish experience with its OA,
and carried some expectations for the shortlists. However, that too ended in disappointment, as I was not
selected.
While the process was depressing, I did not have much to control apart from my own preparation. I opted
to isolate myself2 from distractions and revisit some fundamentals and LeetCode problems in the one week
between the BNY rejection and the Morgan Stanley OA.
Being notified about my interview shortlist at the night of Monday was surely a pleasant surprise, but I pretty
much had only 12 hours to prepare before the interviews formally began.
I hopped on a call with some of my colleagues who had collaborated on one of my résumé projects to help
me explain the project in the event an interviewer wished to see. While this did not happen in my interviews,
other candidates did experience questions on their résumé and their projects, even going as far as presenting
and explaining the codebase within the interview.
The colleagues were kind and also helped me revise CS fundamentals and common HR questions in the same
call, providing a sort of crash-course. I am still grateful of Kartikay and Tanish for that.
After the call, I spent some time midnight solving the top interview LeetCode problems External-Link-Alt. Turns out the
first question in the problemset is Merge Sorted Array itself, which was yet another pleasant surprise the next
day.
The final rush, combined with the advice of colleagues who had cracked internships earlier, was what put me
at my best for the two rounds I appeared in.
Now one peculiarity observed in Morgan Stanley’s results was that they were the first company so far last
season to fully interview all waitlisted candidates. Typically waitlisted candidates are assumed to be kept at
the tail end of the interviews and are expected nine times out of ten to not receive the offer.
However, the trend a lot of companies had been noticing at the time was the inability of candidates to answer
programming and development-based problems that they should be expected to solve given they cleared the
2My method of “isolation” is to socially stay alone for a while.
Page 10 of 12

online assessment. This lackluster performance was probably the reason Morgan Stanley chose to not only
fully interview the waitlisted candidates, but also one of the 4 interns they did select was indeed one of the
original 3 waitlists. This theory is further bolstered by the statistic of them hiring 8 interns in 2024, but
only 4 in 2025.
A possible explanation for this situation well-known unaddressed elephant for online assessments was the
rampant cheating that could be happening at the homes of some candidates, regardless of the proctoring
severity.
OA cheating is nasty and cannot really be avoided. It was one of the supporting factors for why clearing
the OA is a much more difficult task than clearing the interview. Since the alleged cheaters are unable
to clear the interviews, them losing one company and immediately claiming the interview seat of the next
causes a perpetual wastage of a few seats that could have been claimed by an honest candidate.
Other than that, getting selected also requires a lot of fortune. It is practically impossible to predict your
success regardless of how much effort you may have put in. You could literally count the number of ‘pleasant
surprises’ I had this entire experience, and it would demonstrate the power of luck, while every OA failed in
the past would be an example otherwise.
Remember that companies hire with no prior knowledge about the candidates, so if CGPA, OA performance,
Résumé ATS, vibe-check-by-the-assigned-interviewer or any other metric helps them gauge by their
preferences, they may opt for it. Since this is not only out of our knowledge but also our control, attempting
to predict the offer is no better than rolling a dice.
What I would ultimately suggest is to not obsess over any companies, as there is no guarantee of achieving
the offer. However, this should not stop you from practising and revising your skills, as they still improve the
chances of survival. Keep improving yourself until the only way the dice can roll is in your victory.
